blocks.text: **Lectures 9–11.** $X$ can be any number in an interval (a time, a voltage). Find $c$, the CDF, and probabilities.
Question 2 in plain words
**You’ll see:** a PDF or CDF formula, or a story with “uniform”, “exponential” or “normal”. Then parts (a), (b), (c).
**The move: probability is area under the PDF.** The CDF is the area so far:

items: **Accumulate:** $F_X(x)=P(X\le x)$ = the area left of $x$. Same word as the running total in Question 1.
**Differentiate:** the PDF is the slope of the CDF, $f_X=F_X^{\prime}$.
**One exact value has chance $0$:** $P(X=2)=0$. So $<$ and $\le$ give the same answer.

blocks.text: **Short example:** $X$ uniform on $[0,4]$ is flat at $\tfrac14$:
**Which case?** Look for the clue:

rows: “with probability $q$ it is exactly…”, a CDF with a jump

blocks.text: Case 1: find c (total area = 1)
**You’ll see:** “$f_X(x)=c\cdot(\dots)$. Find $c$”, or “show this is a PDF”.
**The move:** the whole area under a PDF is $1$. Write it, set it to $1$, solve:

items: **Find $c$:** integrate $f_X$ over the range where it isn’t $0$ (split at every break), set it to $1$.
**Check:** $f_X\ge0$ everywhere. It may be bigger than $1$, that’s fine.

blocks.text: **Short example:** $f_X(x)=c(1-x^4)$ on $[-1,1]$:

blocks.title: Full example (Practice 02 Q1): $\;f_X(x)=c(1-x^4)$ on $[-1,1]$: find $c$, the CDF, $P(|X|<\tfrac12)$
blocks.text:
Step 1 · **Find $c$:** total area $=1$.

$$
c\Big[x-\frac{x^5}{5}\Big]_{-1}^{1}=\frac{8c}{5}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\frac58
$$

Step 2 · **Accumulate:** the area from $-1$ up to $x$. It’s $0$ before $-1$ and $1$ after $1$.

$$
F_X(x)=\frac58\int_{-1}^{x}(1-t^4)\,dt=\frac58\Big(x-\frac{x^5}{5}+\frac45\Big),\qquad -1\le x\le1
$$

Step 3 · **Rewrite:** $|X|<\tfrac12$ means $-\tfrac12<X<\tfrac12$. The PDF is symmetric, so double the area on $[0,\tfrac12]$.

$$
P\big(|X|<\tfrac12\big)=2\cdot\frac58\Big[x-\frac{x^5}{5}\Big]_0^{1/2}=\frac{79}{128}\approx 0.6172
$$

**Answer:**

$$
c=\frac58,\qquad P\big(|X|<\tfrac12\big)=\frac{79}{128}\approx 0.6172
$$

blocks.title: Shortcut: a triangle or rectangle PDF → use its area formula
blocks.text:
Tutorial 4 Q2: $f(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac14|x-3|$ on $[1,5]$ is a triangle: base $4$, peak height $f(3)=\tfrac12$.

$$
\text{area}=\frac12\cdot4\cdot\frac12=1\quad\checkmark
$$

Unknown height $c$, base $2a$ (Practice 02 Q2):

$$
\frac12\cdot2a\cdot c=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\frac1a
$$

blocks.title: Integrals you’ll need
blocks.text:
Power rule:

$$
\int x^n\,dx=\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}
$$

Exponential (and $e^{-\lambda x}\to0$ as $x\to\infty$):

$$
\int e^{-\lambda x}\,dx=-\frac1\lambda\,e^{-\lambda x}
$$

By parts, for $x\,e^{-x}$ (take $u=x$):

$$
\int x\,e^{-x}\,dx=-(x+1)\,e^{-x}
$$

Shortcut (not from the lectures):

$$
\int_0^{\infty}x^n\,e^{-\lambda x}\,dx=\frac{n!}{\lambda^{n+1}}
$$
Case 2: PDF → CDF → probabilities
**You’ll see:** “find the CDF”, “find the PDF from this CDF”, “find $P(a<X<b)$”.
**The move:** go back and forth between the two, then turn every probability into $F$’s:

items: **Accumulate** (PDF → CDF): the area from the left end up to $x$. Do it piece by piece. $0$ before the range, $1$ after.
**Differentiate** (CDF → PDF): the slope of each piece.
**Rewrite** the probability with $F$’s (card below), then **plug in**.

blocks.title: Rewrite: turn any probability into $F$’s
blocks.text:
Example: $F_X(x)=\tfrac x4$ on $[0,4]$.

Up to $b$:

$$
P(X\le b)=F_X(b)\qquad\qquad P(X\le1)=\frac14
$$

Above $a$:

$$
P(X>a)=1-F_X(a)\qquad\qquad P(X>1)=\frac34
$$

Between:

$$
P(a<X<b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\qquad\qquad P(2<X<3)=\frac34-\frac24=\frac14
$$

One point:

$$
P(X=a)=0
$$
**Short example:** $f_X(x)=\tfrac x2$ on $[0,2]$:

blocks.title: Full example (Lecture 9): read a CDF, $\;F_X(x)=\tfrac x4$ on $[0,4]$
blocks.text:
Step 1 · (a) $P(X\le-1)$: left of the range.

$$
F_X(-1)=0
$$

Step 2 · (b) $P(X\le1)$.

$$
F_X(1)=\frac14
$$

Step 3 · (c) $P(2<X\le3)$: **Rewrite** as a difference.

$$
F_X(3)-F_X(2)=\frac34-\frac24=\frac14
$$

Step 4 · (d) $P(X>1)$: one minus.

$$
1-F_X(1)=\frac34
$$

Step 5 · (e) $P(X=1)$: one point.

$$
0
$$

Step 6 · **Differentiate** for the PDF.

$$
f_X(x)=\frac14,\qquad 0\le x\le4\quad(0\text{ elsewhere})
$$

**Answer:**

$$
0,\ \ \frac14,\ \ \frac14,\ \ \frac34,\ \ 0;\qquad f_X=\frac14\ \text{on }[0,4]
$$

blocks.title: Full example (Tutorial 4 Q2): a triangle PDF, piece by piece
blocks.text:
Step 1 · $f(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac14|x-3|$ on $[1,5]$. Split at the peak: left $\tfrac{x-1}{4}$, right $\tfrac{5-x}{4}$.

Step 2 · **Accumulate**, left half: the area of a small triangle.

$$
F(x)=\int_1^x\frac{t-1}{4}\,dt=\frac{(x-1)^2}{8},\qquad 1\le x\le3
$$

Step 3 · **Accumulate**, right half: $1$ minus the small triangle still to come.

$$
F(x)=1-\frac{(5-x)^2}{8},\qquad 3\le x\le5
$$

Step 4 · **Rewrite** $P(2<X<3.5)$.

$$
F(3.5)-F(2)=\Big(1-\frac{1.5^2}{8}\Big)-\frac18=\frac{19}{32}\approx0.5938
$$

**Answer:**

$$
F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<1\\ \frac{(x-1)^2}{8},&1\le x\le3\\ 1-\frac{(5-x)^2}{8},&3\le x\le5\\ 1,&x>5\end{cases}
$$
Case 3: uniform
**You’ll see:** “uniformly at random between $a$ and $b$”.
**The move:** a flat PDF, so every probability is **length ÷ total length**:

blocks.latex: P(\text{X lands in a piece})=\frac{\text{length of the piece}}{b-a}

blocks.text: **Short example** (Tutorial 2 Q5): a bus comes uniformly between 1:00 and 1:30. Wait at least 10 minutes:

blocks.title: Full example (Tutorial 3 Q1): pick $X$ uniformly in $(0,\tfrac\pi2)$. Chance $\sin X>\cos X$?
blocks.text:
Step 1 · **Spot:** uniform on $(0,\tfrac\pi2)$, total length $\tfrac\pi2$.

Step 2 · **Rewrite** the event: $\sin x$ passes $\cos x$ at $x=\tfrac\pi4$.

$$
\sin X>\cos X\iff X>\frac\pi4
$$

Step 3 · Length ÷ total length.

$$
P=\frac{\frac\pi2-\frac\pi4}{\frac\pi2}=\frac12
$$

**Answer:**

$$
\frac12
$$
Case 4: exponential
**You’ll see:** a lifetime or a waiting time, “exponential with $\lambda=\dots$” ($\lambda$ = the rate, per hour/minute).
**The move:** use the **tail**. You’ll need it more than the CDF:

blocks.latex: f_X(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\qquad F_X(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x},\qquad P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}\qquad(x\ge0)

items: **Spot:** exponential, and read $\lambda$. Given the **mean** instead? Then $\lambda=\dfrac{1}{\text{mean}}$.

blocks.text: **Short example:** lifetime with $\lambda=0.002$ per hour. Lasts at least 500 hours:

blocks.title: Memoryless: $\;P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$
blocks.text:
Time already waited doesn’t matter: an old part is as good as new.

To use it: “already lasted $s$, chance of $t$ more” is a ratio of tails.

$$
\frac{P(X>s+t)}{P(X>s)}=\frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}=e^{-\lambda t}
$$

blocks.title: Full example (Tutorial 4 Q3): a TV tube is 10 years old, $\lambda=0.1$. Chance it lasts another 10?
blocks.text:
Step 1 · **Spot:** exponential, $\lambda=0.1$, and “already lasted” → memoryless.

$$
P(X>20\mid X>10)
$$

Step 2 · **Rewrite** as a ratio of tails.

$$
\frac{P(X>20)}{P(X>10)}=\frac{e^{-2}}{e^{-1}}=e^{-1}
$$

Step 3 · Same as a new tube lasting 10 years.

$$
P(X>10)=e^{-0.1\cdot10}=e^{-1}\approx 0.3679
$$

**Answer:**

$$
e^{-1}\approx 0.3679
$$
Case 5: Gaussian (normal)
**You’ll see:** “normal with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$” (or variance $\sigma^2$): $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$.
**The move:** you can’t integrate the bell curve. **Standardise** to $z$ and read $\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)$ from the table:

items: **Spot:** read $\mu$ and $\sigma$. Given the **variance**? Take its square root first.

blocks.text: **Short example:** $\mu=0$, $\sigma=0.5$, find $P(X<1)$:

blocks.title: Shortcut: a symmetric interval, $\;P(|X-\mu|<k\sigma)=2\Phi(k)-1$
blocks.text:
Both tails are the same size, so take $\Phi(k)$ and remove one tail twice.

$$
\Phi(k)-\Phi(-k)=\Phi(k)-\big(1-\Phi(k)\big)=2\Phi(k)-1
$$

Example: within $1.5\sigma$ of the mean.

$$
2(0.9332)-1=0.8664
$$

blocks.title: Backwards: given a probability, find $x$ $\;\Longrightarrow\;x=\mu+z\sigma$
blocks.text:
Find the $z$ in the table whose $\Phi(z)$ is the probability **below** $x$, then undo the standardising.

$$
x=\mu+z\,\sigma
$$

Top $5\%$ → $95\%$ below → $z=1.645$. Middle $95\%$ → $\Phi(z)=0.975$ → $z=1.96$.

blocks.title: Full example (Lecture 11): sensor error, $\;\mu=0$, $\;\sigma=0.5$. Chance $|X|<0.8$?
Full example (Tutorial 4 Q4): scores $N(500,100^2)$. Which score is the top $10\%$?
blocks.text:
Step 1 · **Rewrite:** top $10\%$ means $90\%$ below.

$$
\Phi\Big(\frac{x-500}{100}\Big)=0.90
$$

Step 2 · **Table, backwards:** $\Phi(1.28)=0.8997$ is closest to $0.90$.

$$
z\approx1.28
$$

Step 3 · Undo the standardising.

$$
x=500+1.28\cdot100=628
$$

**Answer:**

$$
\text{about }628
$$
**Variance or standard deviation?** “$\sigma^2=2.25$” means $\sigma=1.5$. Dividing by $2.25$ is the most common lost mark.

blocks.title: Try it 1 · Case 5 · Blood pressure · Practice 03 Q8
blocks.prompt: Diastolic blood pressure is normal with $\mu=80$, $\sigma=7$ (mm Hg). $\ge95$ is hypertensive; strictly between $89$ and $95$ is mild hypertension. What percent of people are in each group?

steps.explanation: **Standardise** both cut-offs (2 decimals, like the table).

blocks.text: Case 6: mixed (a jump and a ramp)
**You’ll see:** “with probability $q$ it is exactly $x_0$, otherwise it is spread over…”, or a CDF that jumps **and** ramps.
**The move:** the jump is an exact chance. The spread part only has the **leftover** area $1-q$:

items: **Jump:** $P(X=x_0)=q$ (or read the jump size off the CDF).
**Rewrite:** any probability = the jumps inside the range + the area over the range.

blocks.text: **Short example:** signal lost ($X=0$) with chance $0.2$, otherwise uniform on $(0,10)$:

blocks.title: Full example (Lectures 10–11): received signal level, the CDF
blocks.text:
Step 1 · **Jump** at $0$: the lost signal.

$$
P(X=0)=0.2
$$

Step 2 · **Spread:** uniform on $(0,10)$ scaled by $0.8$.

$$
f(x)=0.8\cdot\frac1{10}=0.08,\qquad 0<x<10
$$

Step 3 · **Accumulate:** jump first, then the ramp.

$$
F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0\\ 0.2+0.08x,&0\le x<10\\ 1,&x\ge10\end{cases}
$$

Step 4 · **Rewrite** $P(2<X<5)$: the jump at $0$ isn’t inside, so only area.

$$
F_X(5)-F_X(2)=0.6-0.36=0.24
$$

**Answer:**

$$
\text{jump }0.2\text{ at }0,\ \text{then a ramp up to }1\text{ at }x=10
$$

**Discrete = all jumps, continuous = all slope, mixed = both.**

blocks.title: Try it 2 · Case 6 · Daily rainfall
blocks.prompt: On a given day it doesn’t rain with probability $0.6$ ($X=0$). If it rains, the amount $X$ (mm) is exponential with $\lambda=0.5$. (a) Find the CDF of $X$. (b) Find $P(X>2)$. (c) Find $P(X\le1)$.

steps.explanation: **Spot:** an exact value with chance $0.6$, plus a spread → Case 6.
(a) **Jump** of $0.6$ at $0$, then **spread:** the exponential CDF scaled by $0.4$.
(b) **Rewrite:** only rainy days can go above 2. Exponential tail times $0.4$.

blocks.text: Practice Questions

**Question 2 is always these cases, in parts (a), (b), (c).** Spot the clue, run its steps:

1. **Find $c$:** total area $=1$ (triangle/rectangle: area formula).
2. **PDF ↔ CDF:** Accumulate (area so far), Differentiate (slope), Rewrite with $F$'s.
3. **Uniform:** length ÷ total length.
4. **Exponential:** $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$; “already lasted” → memoryless.
5. **Gaussian:** $z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ → $\Phi$ table; $\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)$; backwards $x=\mu+z\sigma$.
6. **Mixed:** jump = exact chance; spread × $(1-q)$; add jumps + area.
Test-style, easy → hard. Solve on paper first, then open the solution.

blocks.title: Question 1 · Case 3 · Uniform · Tutorial 4 Q5
blocks.prompt: Flights leave every half hour (9:00, 9:30, 10:00, …). A passenger arrives at a uniform random time between 8:45 and 9:45 A.M. Find the probability the passenger waits (a) **at most 10 minutes**, (b) **at least 15 minutes**.

steps.explanation: **Type:** uniform → Case 3. $T$ = minutes after 8:45, total length $60$. Flights leave at $T=15,\ 45,\ 75$.
(a) **Rewrite:** wait $\le10$ means arriving in the 10 minutes before a flight.
(b) **Rewrite:** wait $\ge15$ means the next flight is 15+ minutes away.

blocks.title: Question 3 · Case 2 · CDF → probabilities and PDF · Practice 02 Q4
blocks.prompt:
The Rayleigh random variable $R$ has CDF

$$
F_R(r)=\begin{cases}0,&r<0\\ 1-e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},&r\ge0\end{cases}
$$

(a) Find $P(\sigma\le R\le2\sigma)$ and $P(R>3\sigma)$. (b) Find the PDF of $R$.

steps.explanation: (a) **Rewrite** as a difference. $\sigma$ cancels in each power.

blocks.title: Question 4 · Case 1 + 2 · Find $c$, then the CDF · Tutorial 5 Q5
blocks.prompt: $X$ has PDF $f_X(x)=Cx^2$ for $|x|\le1$, and $0$ otherwise. (a) Find $C$. (b) Find the CDF. (c) Find $P(X>\tfrac12)$ and $P(|X|<\tfrac12)$.

steps.explanation: **Rewrite** as a difference. Small, because the PDF is near $0$ around $x=0$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** unknown constant → Case 1. First the integral, **by parts** ($u=x$, $dv=e^{-x}dx$):

blocks.title: Question 6 · Case 1 + 2 · a triangle, then work backwards · Practice 02 Q2
blocks.prompt: $X$ has a triangle PDF: $0$ at $x=-a$, peak height $c$ at $x=0$, back to $0$ at $x=a$. (a) Find $c$ and $f_X(x)$. (b) Find the CDF. (c) Find $b$ with $P(|X|<b)=\tfrac12$.

steps.explanation: (a) **Type:** unknown height → Case 1. **Find $c$** with the triangle shortcut: base $2a$, height $c$.
The two sides are straight lines down from the peak.
(b) **Accumulate:** left half = a small triangle; right half = $1$ minus the small triangle still to come.

steps.explanation: **Type:** normal → Case 5. **Spot:** that’s the variance, so take the root.
(a) $500$ is the centre: half the bell is below it.

blocks.title: Question 9 · Case 6 · a CDF with two jumps
blocks.prompt:
A clipped sensor reading $X$ has CDF

$$
F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<0\\ 0.25+\tfrac x2,&0\le x<1\\ 1,&x\ge1\end{cases}
$$

(a) Why is $X$ mixed? (b) Find $P(X=0)$ and $P(X=1)$. (c) Find $P(0<X<1)$ and $P(X\le0.5)$. (d) Find the PDF of the spread part.

steps.explanation: (a) **Type:** $F$ jumps (exact values with real chance) **and** ramps → Case 6.
(b) **Jump** sizes. At $1$, $F$ goes from $0.25+0.5=0.75$ up to $1$.
(c) **Rewrite:** only the ramp is strictly inside $(0,1)$.

blocks.title: Question 10 · Case 6 · Practice 02 Q3
blocks.prompt:
$X$ has CDF

$$
F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<-1\\ \tfrac13+\tfrac23(x+1)^2,&-1\le x\le0\\ 1,&x>0\end{cases}
$$

Find the probabilities of $A=\{X>\tfrac13\}$, $B=\{|X|\ge1\}$, $C=\{|X-\tfrac13|<1\}$, $D=\{X<0\}$.

steps.explanation: **Type:** $F$ jumps from $0$ to $\tfrac13$ at $x=-1$, then rises smoothly → Case 6.
$A$: **Rewrite** as one minus. $X$ is never above $0$.
